newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian court rules against opposition in 5 areas.
newsitem.headline: Serbian court rules against opposition in 5 areas.

text.p: The Serbian Supreme Court began handing down verdicts on disputed local elections, its first rulings on individual electoral districts going against the opposition coalition, an opposition official said.

"The court has ruled on five out of 46 electoral districts (in which results are being reviewed) and dismissed the opposition's complaints," the official of the Democratic Party, a member of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, said late on Saturday.

"Having in view the fact that our complaints to the court are identical for all 46 electoral districts, we have no reason to believe the court will rule in any different way for the remaining 41," he said.
The official confirmed an earlier report by independent Belgrade radio B-92 that the Court had started turning down the appeals. The report could not immediately be officially confirmed.

The radio quoted Milica Nedeljkovic, Zajedno's representative in the City Election Commission, as saying: "The Commission has received rulings by the Court endorsing an earlier decision by a lower court to annul elections results in five districts."

Zajedno claimed victory in Belgrade and another 14 of Serbia's biggest towns in local elections on November 17, but the ruling Socialist Party said there had been voting irregularities and a Belgrade municipal court annulled election results in the capital.
The opposition claimed it had won 60 out of 110 seats in the Belgrade city assembly.
The opposition then lodged a plea to the Supreme Court.
Before the result of last month's elections was revoked, the opposition had won control of the capital, wresting it from left-wingers for the first time in half a century.
If the Supreme Court rules against Zajedno for the remaining districts, it is bound to infuriate tens of thousands of people who have staged unprecedented protests for the past 18 days in Belgrade.
The annulment of the opposition victories drew sharp criticism from the West, which has piled pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to respect democracy.
The Court's ruling comes hours after Milosevic was reported to be struggling to disengage himself from opposition charges of election-rigging.

About 150,000 people turned out on chilly Belgrade streets on Saturday for the 18th day of protest marches. Tens of thousands of others marched in Nis, Kragujevac, Valjevo, Sevojno, Leskovac and Novi Sad.
B-92 reported that police had arrested Dejan Bulatovic, a student from Sid, who carried at Saturday's demonstrations in Belgrade en effigy of Milosevic dressed in striped prison clothes.
Milosevic told a U.S. media rights activist on saturday that he would respect the Supreme Court's decision.
"He said he would obey what the Supreme Court decides," the president of the U.S. Committee for the Protection of Journalists, Kati Morton, told Reuters after meeting Milosevic.

The decision to revoke the opposition victory has turned into a political catastrophe for Milosevic, mobilising daily demonstrations by up to 150,000 people against his nine-year rule and destroying his electoral credibility.
The United States has led a Western campaign to force Milosevic to honour the polls and open talks with Zajedno.
The European Union decided to refuse Belgrade preferential trade terms granted to its Balkan neighbours.
The mood on Belgrade streets was euphoric as the conviction grew that the sustained protests had inflicted severe damage on Milosevic's rule.
A poll in NIN magazine showed Milosevic was suffering politically, with a fall in his public support from 26 percent to an all-time low of 16.5 percent since the protests began.
